title: Why Arab armies don't win wars - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: A review of Kenneth Pollack's Armies of Sand argues that Arab militaries' chronic underperformance despite superior men and materiel stems less from Soviet doctrine or politicization than from cultural patterns (deference to authority, shame avoidance, rote-learning education) that also pervade Arab bureaucracies and hamper regional economic reform.

insights.claim: In the 1967 Six-Day War, Israel destroyed 298 of Egypt's 420 combat aircraft on the ground while Egyptian commanders reported the opposite to Nasser, and the Arab coalition lost 70,000 square kilometers despite fielding more troops, tanks and aircraft.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Numerical and hardware superiority is a poor predictor of Middle East war outcomes; weight force quality and command culture when assessing regional conflict risk.
insights.quote: the Israelis had bombed 298 of Egypt’s 420 combat aircraft on the tarmac
insights.locator: Nasser’s commanders hadn’t been entirely honest

insights.claim: Arab military failure is not simply a function of Israeli sophistication: Gaddafi's Libya lost repeatedly to impoverished Chad, and Saddam Hussein's offensive against Iran was among the weakest of the past century.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Underperformance is structural across opponents, so do not assume Arab states' arms purchases translate into regional deterrence.
insights.quote: one of the most pathetic military offensives of the past century
insights.locator: In Armies of Sand, former CIA analyst

insights.claim: Soviet-style doctrine emphasizing preplanned operations and centralized control caused Arab officers to freeze when battlefields shifted, as when Syrian troops paused after breaking through on the Golan Heights in 1973, letting Israeli reserves retake the ground.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Rigid, centrally planned forces fail to exploit breakthroughs; initial successes by such forces are often transient.
insights.locator: There are a few common theories among experts

insights.claim: Coup-fearing Arab leaders politicized their militaries through loyalty promotions and purges; Saddam Hussein at one point ran as many as sixteen security services that largely spied on each other.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Coup-proofing trades battlefield effectiveness for regime survival, a durable feature of authoritarian Middle East states.

insights.claim: Pollack rejects doctrine and politicization as root causes because Cuba and North Korea used Soviet doctrine yet fought creditably, and Egypt's performance stayed dismal even after substantial depoliticization in the 1970s.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reforms targeting doctrine or civil-military relations alone are unlikely to fix Arab military effectiveness.

themes.theme: Culture and education as root cause

insights.claim: Pollack attributes Arab military failure to cultural patterns: deference to authority, in-group loyalty, a premium on personal honor and horror of shame, which lead commanders to misreport and junior officers to follow obsolete orders.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Expect information flows up Arab chains of command to be distorted by shame avoidance; discount official battlefield claims.
insights.quote: deference to authority, loyalty to the in-group over outsiders, a premium on personal honor, and horror of shame
insights.locator: Instead, he argues that these failures

insights.claim: Mass Arab public school systems built in the 1950s-60s kept the memorization-based pedagogy of Quranic schools, and that rote-learning habit carries into military training built on rehearsing pre-scripted maneuvers.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Human-capital constraints from rote-learning education limit adaptive capacity across militaries and firms in the region.
insights.locator: When governments built mass public school systems

insights.claim: An American trainer said Egypt's elite F-16 pilots knew in advance where to turn, where to fake firing and who would win their exercises, and got upset when anyone deviated from the script.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Advanced Western weapons sales to Arab states may deliver far less real capability than their spec sheets suggest.
insights.quote: they know where to turn, and where to pretend to fire munitions, and who is going to win
insights.locator: An American trainer working with Egypt’s elite

insights.claim: Hezbollah became a highly capable force after downsizing following the Lebanese Civil War, retaining only a small minority of culturally atypical fighters proven in battle.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Small, selectively filtered non-state forces can outperform large Arab state militaries; weigh them more heavily in regional risk assessments.
insights.locator: The exceptions largely support Pollack’s case

insights.claim: At its 2014 peak, Islamic State drew its most gifted commanders from Chechens, Uzbeks and Tajiks rather than Arab recruits.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Foreign fighter cadres, not local mass, drive jihadist battlefield effectiveness; track their flows as a leading indicator.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, Islamic State, at its 2014 peak

insights.claim: In a study of Egyptian, Saudi and Sudanese bureaucracies, 90 percent of senior officials deemed their subordinates unqualified to innovate, reflecting top-concentrated authority and no reward for risk-taking.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Centralized, risk-averse management culture is a hidden execution risk for Gulf and Egyptian state-led diversification programs.
insights.locator: In most Arab offices and government ministries

insights.claim: The same hierarchical, shame-averse traits seen in Arab armies pervade Middle Eastern banks and government ministries and continue to impede regional social and economic reform.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Discount timelines for Middle East economic reform agendas where cultural-institutional change is required, not just capital.
insights.locator: Anyone who has interacted with a bank
